# Python packaging with Digital Rights Management 101

![Python](data:image/webp;base64,)

It's been a while since I looked into Python packaging seeing I found home using a combination of `uv`
version and package management tools in combination with `hatch` extensible build-system and
found that I can experiment with many things in this area just by adjusting `hatchling` packages used,
for example an ahead-of-time compiled library using `mypyc`, or completely drop it and use `maturin`
for oxidation Python 🐍 with Rust 🦀 programming underneath the hood.

Someone handed me an interesting task recently about obfuscation source code and setting up private
PyPI registry so I thought that I should revisit this area. While obfuscation by itself is an easy task,
combining it with licensing agreement, registry authentication and binary expiration are all profitable
prospects on their own and should be explored thoroughly.

Normally I like to open source my code and make money on the expertise built along the way, the thought
of having 3 - 4 giant companies always indexing my work without accredition and offering patchwork
consultation to the mass has shifted the equation a fair bit. I believe that agreement between parties
and limiting source leakage does in fact allow for seamless distributions rather than subscription-based
consulting fees, and an avenue not expounded upon enought.

To my surprise, there are no currently active `hatchling` package that obfuscates the codebase for distribution.
I believe `PyArmor` fits the bill in terms of basic obfuscation, but this also means adjusting the right build
tool for it without getting in the way of development. Some online suggestions point that adding customized
`build-system` section to your `pyproject.toml` as such does the trick, but after some trial and error, this
does not fit the bill at all.

```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=61.0.0", "wheel", "pyarmor>=7.2.0"]
build-backend = "pyarmor.build_meta"
```

The best step forward is to modernize this tool chain by creating my own open source obfuscation extension
on either `hatchling` or `uv` based on my past experimentation with `mypyc` and see if these can be combined.

Tests will include attempts at reverse engineering the package and property-based verification that the
obfuscation is a one-way street. Should be fun.
